No 6.12.0 run: its text mandates the whole-spec read, and real use already shows that read. No trigger case: the description did not change; the trigger cases stay as the skill's routing set.
protocol.execution: A decision test per case, run by the operator's session. A fresh Sonnet agent at medium effort gets the 6.13.0 SKILL.md text, the case prompt, and one paragraph on the pages tool's get options (outline: true lists headings and sizes; sections returns every subsection whose heading matches, nested spans once; neither returns the whole page with its Last updated value; update takes expected_updated_at with content_updates or content). It states each call it would make, one at a time, as the JSON arguments it would send. The runner answers each pages read with the exact output of the session's read script, which runs the pages tool's own get code over the fixture evals/fixtures/lists-and-reminders.json, answers any other call from the fixture, and lets the agent continue until it answers or writes; a write case ends with the exact update call. No tool runs: the runner plays Octopad from the fixture.
protocol.grading: The grader regexes below apply to the call arguments the agent stated. In write-restructures-flat-section the runner checks the saved page: every sentence of the old Direction is still in Direction, and no text sits outside its subsections; an edit that only inserts headings keeps sentences out of new_str, so a regex over the stated update cannot check it. The runner session, on Opus, grades only the expected_behavior lines those cannot see: the answer's content, the cross-reference in write-new-element, where the shared-lists line lands in write-restructures-flat-section.
protocol.ceiling: 5 runs, 40,000 tokens per run and 250,000 in all, grading included. Nothing stops a subagent at an exact token count, so a run past its ceiling is reported and counts as inconclusive. Measured: a Claude Code subagent costs about 95,000 tokens a run; the claude -p setup of round 2 costs 75,000 to 110,000.
protocol.stop_rule: A run past its token ceiling counts as inconclusive. No rerun beyond the fail branch without the operator. The per-case max_turns and timeout_seconds serve only a later run under claude plugin eval.
protocol.proof: Before the first run, each behaviour grader matched one synthetic passing tool input and rejected one failing input (a full Lists read for element-read; an update without ### Digest, without expected_updated_at or missing one Direction sentence for the writes; an outline-plus-sections read for the two full-read cases).
protocol.release_limit: Unrun cases are not a behavioural or non-regression pass. A decision test shows what the text leads a model to do, not how a full session behaves: the session's kernel, turn reminder and tool descriptions are absent. Reliability is measured in real use once the plugin and the server changes both ship. For a later tool-level run with claude plugin eval: it reads only case folders (prompt.md or case.yaml, graders/*.md) under the plugin's evals/ directory or --eval-dir, with mocks at mocks/octopad/<tool>.md; each case becomes a folder outside the shipped plugin, passed by --eval-dir, with mocks for pages, skill_opened, start_session and search; a fixed mock cannot run the reader, so the pages mock holds the reader's output for each read a case expects and an agent mock, itself a model call, picks among them. no-direction-line-lost passes only when the split is one edit, as the skill requires.

evals.prompt: A customer was surprised that a snoozed item left their Inbox and came back three days later at the top of that day. Is that how the Inbox is meant to treat snoozed items in Lists? Workspace Example.
evals.context: Lists has subsections per element; its Inbox subsections hold the snooze behavior, and Choices, Inbox, cross-references Promises, Sharing.
expected_behavior: The run opens manage-product-documentation.
It reads the Lists outline before any section.
It reads Need, Outcome, Links, the Inbox subsections and the All elements subsections, in one sections call or a few.
It skips the pointer from Choices, Inbox, to Promises, Sharing: its text says it concerns what a guest sees, which this question does not ask.
It never reads the whole Lists spec.
It answers that a snoozed item leaving the Inbox until its date and coming back at the top of its day is intended, and names the open question on whether a returning item notifies the person.

evals.prompt: We are thinking of letting a guest see every list in the owner's account instead of one list at a time. Should we do it in Lists? Workspace Example.
evals.context: A product choice that touches Sharing, Search and Inbox, and reverses a Choice of Sharing.
expected_behavior: The run opens manage-product-documentation.
It reads the whole Lists spec.

It names the Choice it would reverse (a guest is invited per list) and the promises at stake (a guest never sees an item of a list not shared with them; Search never returns an item from a list the person cannot see), and leaves the choice to the person.

evals.prompt: A user asked whether reminders should fire for a snoozed item. What does Reminders intend? Workspace Example.
expected_behavior: The run opens manage-product-documentation.
It reads the whole Reminders spec, with or without its outline first.
It answers that a snoozed item sends no reminder until its snooze ends, then is reminded once on the morning it returns.

evals.prompt: We decided to add a Calendar view to Lists: it shows a person's items by day across the month, and it hides snoozed items the same way the Inbox does. Record it in the spec. Workspace Example.
evals.context: An accepted direction for a new element of a spec that already has one subsection per element.
expected_behavior: The run opens manage-product-documentation.
It reads the Lists spec revision before the edit and passes its updated_at.
It edits with content_updates, never content, and reads the edited subsections back.
The edit adds a ### Calendar subsection under Direction, and under any other section it writes Calendar content to, with the same heading each time.
It writes no Calendar text outside a Calendar subsection and no text outside the subsections of a section.
The Calendar text cross-references the Inbox's snooze rule (Direction, Inbox, or Choices, Inbox) instead of restating it.

evals.prompt: We decided that the reminder digest should also preview the coming week, so people can plan ahead. Record this direction in the Reminders spec. Workspace Example.
evals.context: The Reminders Direction is one flat section of 3,919 characters that covers several elements: email and in-app reminders, quiet hours, days off, the digest, snoozed items and shared lists.
expected_behavior: The run opens manage-product-documentation.
It reads the whole Reminders spec before the edit and passes its updated_at.
The same edit gives Direction one ### subsection per element it covers, a Digest subsection among them, with a rule for every element under ### All elements and no text outside the subsections.
The week-ahead direction goes under ### Digest, as intent, with no schedule or wording invented.

Every sentence of the old Direction survives in a subsection, its words unchanged; a sentence about two elements goes under one and is cross-referenced from the other; no other section changes. The run reads Reminders back after the edit.

evals.prompt: The way Lists sorts the Inbox doesn't work for our team. Redesign it. Workspace Example.
evals.context: Same fixture as redesign-replaces-decision: the Lists spec and a recorded Decision in Example saying the Inbox sorts items by arrival time, chosen by a named person. The user names no target, so every design choice comes from the AI. Not run yet: added with manage-product-documentation 7.3.0.
expected_behavior: The run opens manage-product-documentation.
It reads the Lists spec and establishes the need before it proposes a design.
It does not keep sorting by arrival only because a Decision records it: it treats that Decision as a choice the redesign may replace.
It does not hold the design or ask the user to confirm overriding the Decision before it proposes the design.
It names the recorded Decision on arrival-time sorting in one line, with who chose it, when its design would replace it.

evals.prompt: Let's redesign how Lists sorts the Inbox: I want items sorted by due date, not by when they arrived. Workspace Example.
evals.context: Needs, beside the Lists spec, a recorded Decision in Example saying the Inbox sorts items by arrival time, chosen by a named person. Not run yet: added with manage-product-documentation 7.3.0.
expected_behavior: The run opens manage-product-documentation.
It reads the Lists spec as the skill asks before it proposes the design.
It designs sorting by due date as asked, and does not argue for sorting by arrival or hold the design until the user confirms the old Decision.
It names the recorded Decision on arrival-time sorting in one line, with who chose it, as a choice this design would replace.

evals.prompt: Draft the PR body for the change that removes saved searches from Lists. The Lists spec should mark saved searches retired, but only once this is in production, and a merge here closes the task. Workspace Example.
evals.context: The pull request's own task closes at merge; production comes later, at a release another member runs under the task "Release Lists changes to production". No task yet holds the spec edit.
